title: scope the six CI jobs that inherit a write GITHUB_TOKEN they never use
debugSession: .harness/debug/resolved/workflow-token-least-authority.md (LOCAL ONLY — `.harness/.gitignore` ignores `debug/`, so the harness-debugging session file is not committed by design; its investigation log, hypothesis and resolution are reproduced in this record and in the PR body)
rootCause: Not the six files individually. GitHub resolves a job's token scopes job-level > workflow-level > REPOSITORY DEFAULT, and this repository's default is verifiably `write` (`gh api repos/:owner/:repo/actions/permissions/workflow` returns {"default_workflow_permissions":"write","can_approve_pull_request_reviews":true}). 16 of the 22 workflow files already declared `permissions: contents: read`, and `git log -S"permissions:"` shows each acquired it in the commit that authored it — so the convention was real but enforced only by author memory. No gate anywhere read the workflow directory and failed on an undeclared job, so the six files written without one silently inherited write on every scope, and any seventh would have too. Worst exposure: smoke-test.yml:smoke triggers on `workflow_run` (always evaluated in the default-branch context with the full token) and `npm install -g`s then dynamically imports eight freshly published packages — third-party code executing on a runner holding a write-scoped repository token.
fix: `contents: read` on all six jobs, plus the missing gate. benchmark.yml, harness.yml, openapi-drift-check.yml and smoke-test.yml take a workflow-ROOT block (single-job files, matching the existing 16-file convention). ci.yml takes JOB-LEVEL blocks on `changeset-check` and `build-and-test` only. A root block was rejected because with NO root block, a future job added to ci.yml that forgets `permissions:` has no declaration at either level and reds the new test, whereas a root `contents: read` would silently absorb it. The ci.yml diff is +16/-0 and refresh-baselines / comprehension-refresh are byte-identical to base.
verification: Fails-before / passes-after proven under the exact CI command (`node --test 'tests/scripts/*.test.mjs'`, Node 22): 91 pass / 1 fail at base with the test present, 92 pass / 0 fail with the fix applied. The failing assertion names all six jobs. Effective permissions were re-derived for all 31 jobs after the fix and diffed against base: exactly 6 lines change (undefined -> {contents: read}); the other 25 jobs are byte-identical. The hardened test was additionally proven to catch both evasions a bare existence check would miss: a new workflow landing with `permissions: write-all`, and a silent widening of one of the six back to `contents: write` — both go red.
assumptions: `contents: read` was assessed SUFFICIENT for all six jobs by STEP INSPECTION, not by observing a run: every step is checkout / setup-node / pnpm install / build / run a repo script, and grep for `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `gh `, `github-token` and `secrets.` across the four single-job files returns zero hits. Inside ci.yml's two jobs the only secret is CODECOV_TOKEN, a separate repository secret that `permissions:` does not scope.

The least-authority property is asserted BY CONSTRUCTION rather than demonstrated by an observed denied write. The property is the absence of a write these jobs never attempt, and an absence emits no runtime signal — so no failing-then-passing runtime test for it can exist. Green CI proves the `permissions:` blocks do not BREAK the jobs; it does not prove the control.

The repository-level `default_workflow_permissions` remains `write`. Flipping it to `read` would close this class permanently, including for workflows not yet written, but it is a GitHub SETTINGS change that no pull request can carry. It is a required human action this change did NOT perform.

Scoped strictly to the six undeclared jobs. The 16 already-compliant files and the jobs that genuinely write (refresh-baselines, comprehension-refresh, release, snapshot, roadmap-auto-done, holiday-confidence-track, main-health, docker, required-review, rollback-propose) were left exactly as found; the new test pins the first two so a later narrowing reds a test instead of main.

Fork PRs already receive a read-only token regardless of `default_workflow_permissions`, so this change's benefit lands on same-repo PRs, `push: main`, and the `workflow_run` smoke job — which is also the highest-exposure of the six.
securityReview: harness-security-reviewer run over the diff: PASS / approve, zero critical findings. It independently re-derived the repo default (`write`), confirmed no step in any of the six ever receives GITHUB_TOKEN, and confirmed actions/upload-artifact and codecov-action need neither `contents: write` nor `id-token: write` (codecov's `use_oidc` defaults false; artifact/cache I/O uses ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN, which `permissions:` does not govern — proven in-repo by refresh-baselines, which already has `actions: none` and runs cache/download-artifact green). It raised two IMPORTANT holes in the regression test itself, BOTH FIXED IN THIS CHANGE: the invariant was an existence check (satisfiable by `permissions: write-all`) and it ratcheted only one way (nothing stopped the six newly scoped readers being widened back to write). Both are closed by the WRITERS allowlist + value comparison. It also corrected a partly-false rationale in the ci.yml comment, which has been rewritten.
parkedFollowUps: NOT FIXED HERE — deliberately parked to avoid growing the fix. smoke-test.yml's `actions/checkout@v6` leaves `persist-credentials` at its default `true`, writing GITHUB_TOKEN into the workspace .git/config as an http.extraheader; the job then `npm install`s and executes lifecycle scripts from eight freshly published registry tarballs on that same runner. This change collapses the SEVERITY of that exposure (the persisted token is now read-only) but not the exposure itself. Remedy is one line — `persist-credentials: false` — but it is a distinct control from token scoping and changes checkout behaviour, so it belongs in its own change.

NOT A FINDING, noted by the reviewer: ci.yml's codecov step sets `fail_ci_if_error: false`, so a green CI run is not evidence the Codecov upload still works. Do not cite CI green as proof of that particular step.
